title: The Curriculum Compression Problem
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen argues that curriculum databases and adaptive platforms that start with maths and then expand to other subjects tend to fail because different subjects require fundamentally different theories of structure. She frames every curriculum as a lossy compression of knowledge and shows how the compression problem varies. In maths the domain supplies real prerequisite constraints, while in history almost all structure is imposed by the designer and there is a second layer of disciplinary reasoning that a dependency graph cannot capture. Science sits in between, combining concepts, practices and messy biological generalisations that require judgement about productive simplification. Her central distinction is between a curriculum graph, which is a designed object, and a knowledge graph, which would reflect the domain itself, and she concludes that the database model should vary by subject, not just the content.
points: All curricula are lossy compressions of knowledge, but the kind of compression problem differs by subject.
Maths prerequisite graphs work because dependencies are properties of the mathematics, though even there the result is a designed curriculum graph rather than a pure knowledge graph.
History curricula must coordinate substantive knowledge and disciplinary reasoning and be robust to forgetting, which a dependency graph cannot express.
Science combines concepts with practices and must decide which simplifications are generative and which become misconceptions.
Maths-first platforms silently distort other subjects by pouring different content into the same container, so the structure itself must vary by subject.
quotes: All curricula are lossy compressions. You take knowledge that is, in reality, distributed, contextual, and uneven, and you squeeze it into a scope and sequence that can be taught in a classroom over a year. Something always gets lost.

If a student doesn’t understand place value, multi-digit arithmetic becomes procedural guesswork. If fractions aren’t understood as numbers, ratio and proportion are meaningless. These dependencies are properties of the mathematics, not just choices a curriculum designer made.

History does not work like this. There are some dependencies — you probably need to know something about the Roman Republic before you can make sense of its fall — but the domain offers almost no intrinsic prerequisite structure. You can teach the French Revolution before or after the American Revolution; the choice is pedagogical, not logical. Nearly all the structure in a history curriculum is imposed by the designer, not discovered in the domain.

The question is not mainly “what must be known before what?” but “what kinds of residual understanding are we trying to leave behind?” Which narratives survive partial forgetting? Which causal patterns stick? Which interpretive habits become second nature? A dependency graph has nothing to say about this, because it only represents what must come first and not what must endure.

There are the concepts themselves (what scientists know), and there are the disciplinary practices (what scientists do: designing experiments, constructing explanations, arguing from evidence, developing new ideas). These are different knowledge types that develop somewhat independently: a student can understand energy concepts without being able to design an investigation, and vice versa.
The mistake these systems make is not that they get maths wrong. They usually get maths right. The mistake is subtler: they confuse a curriculum graph with a knowledge graph.

What happens with maths-first platforms is that the domain constraint is so strong it feels like pure discovery. The team builds a structure for maths, it works, and they assume the structure generalises. When they expand into other subjects, the same architecture becomes the default
